For b=3 and (e_1,e_2,e_3)=(1,1,6), the divisibility hypothesis holds for every positive integer d: for d=1,2,3 both sides are equal, and for d>=4 the right-hand side is 0. But in S=Q[y_1,y_2,y_3] with weighted degrees deg(y_i)=i, the homogeneous degree-1 subspace is one-dimensional, spanned by y_1. Hence any homogeneous u_1,u_2 of degree 1 are proportional. If u_1=0 then the sequence is not regular; if u_1!=0 then u_2 lies in (u_1), so its image in S/(u_1) is 0, which is not a non-zero-divisor in the nonzero ring S/(u_1). Therefore no regular sequence u_1,u_2,u_3 with degrees 1,1,6 exists.

shared_context.content: For a finite multiset lambda of integers, wt(lambda) denotes the sum of its elements. In the root theorem this quantity is written |lambda|; for an ordinary set S, |S| still means cardinality.

shared_context.content: If F(q) = sum_{n >= 0} c_n q^n is a formal power series, then [q^j]F(q) denotes c_j.

shared_context.content: In a commutative ring R, an ordered finite list g_1,...,g_n is a regular sequence if for each i, the image of g_i is not a zero-divisor in R/(g_1,...,g_{i-1}); the empty list is allowed.
shared_context.label: Regular sequence

shared_context.content: If A = direct_sum_{n >= 0} A_n is a graded Q-vector space with each A_n finite-dimensional, then Hilb_A(q) := sum_{n >= 0} (dim_Q A_n) q^n.

strategy_summary: Realize the interval product as the Hilbert series of a graded complete intersection in a weighted polynomial ring. The divisibility-count hypothesis is used only in one bottleneck algebraic realization lemma. Once that realization is available, the coefficient of q^j becomes a graded dimension and is therefore nonnegative. A separate expansion lemma identifies the same coefficient with the signed count of X_j, and a finite-set pairing lemma converts the resulting excess of even-parity elements into the required involution on X_j.
